Specifically she pulls the lessons learned from earlier warehouse and IT integration projects, any industry benchmarks the company has used (for example typical delay rates for automation installs), and records of past risk events with their real costs and how long they took. She then reviews the templates for a risk register and a probability-and-impact scale. The reason to do this first is that the team should not invent its starting assumptions from memory. A common mistake is to brainstorm risks in a workshop without checking what already went wrong on similar work, which leads to a register that misses the known problem areas, such as vendor installation slippage. The consequence for a live warehouse system is that a missed integration risk can stop goods movement on the floor once the system is switched on.

The threshold is a measurable line that tells the team when a risk must be escalated, and it must sit inside the company's risk appetite. Because the two directors disagree and no written appetite exists, Priya should not choose between their numbers herself. She should document both positions, show the steering committee how each threshold would change the number of escalated risks using her historical data, and ask the sponsor to lead a conflict resolution session with both directors. The decision to confirm is the organisation-level risk appetite statement, including the escalation threshold for each risk category, and the sponsor, as the accountable executive, should approve it in writing. Until then Priya uses the lower of the two thresholds as an interim safety setting and labels it provisional. A common mistake is to let the stricter threshold quietly become policy or to let the project team absorb a decision that belongs to senior leaders. The consequence is that a risk above the board limit could be handled inside the project and never reach the people able to fund a response.

A risk breakdown structure (RBS) is a hierarchy that groups all possible risk sources in a project into categories and sub-categories, so nothing is overlooked and risks can be reported by source. For this warehouse project a sensible top level is technical (equipment and software integration), external (suppliers, labour market, regulation), organizational (funding, staffing, change readiness), and project management (schedule, scope, communication). Each top-level category then splits into sources such as vendor installation, data migration, and site access. Priya should then document the roles and responsibilities in a RACI matrix (a chart showing who is Responsible for doing a task, Accountable for the result, Consulted before decisions, and Informed afterwards). The RACI assigns each RBS category to a named owner. A common mistake is to build a long RBS but leave ownership blank, so risks have no one acting on them. The consequence is that a known supplier delay can sit unmanaged until the installation date slips.

The risk communication plan states who receives what risk information, how often, and in what format. For the steering committee, which needs decisions rather than detail, Priya should give a short monthly summary of the top risks, their thresholds, any breaches, and the decisions needed, using the approved risk appetite statement as the reference point. For the site operations team, which will run the system daily, she should give shorter, practical updates tied to their work, such as cutover dates and system downtime windows, and she should run a brief walk-through of the risk register at each sprint review. One risk principle to coach the operations team on is that risk is about uncertainty in both directions, so an early delivery or a quicker supplier can also be a risk to be planned for, not just a delay. A common mistake is to send the same report to everyone, which leads to busy executives ignoring the detail and floor staff not understanding why a change matters to them.

scenarios.title: Tallow Bay Logistics warehouse stock system migration
scenarios.scenario: Tallow Bay Logistics is a fictional regional freight company moving its warehouse stock-tracking system from an old on-site server to a cloud-hosted service within nine months. You have just become the project manager. Your team lead hands you three raw inputs. First, an assumption log. An assumption is something the team accepts as true without proof yet, and a constraint is a fixed limit the project must work within. The log lists these items: the cloud vendor will deliver the new handheld scanners by week 10 (assumption); the export tool will move all 1.2 million item records in a single pass without splitting them into batches (assumption); the nightly stock sync must finish within a six-hour window because the warehouse opens at 5 a.m. (constraint); and the budget cannot rise above its approved amount (constraint). Second, a telemetry export. Telemetry means automatic measurements a system records about itself, such as how long a scheduled job takes to run. The nightly sync job averaged 4 hours 10 minutes over the past six weeks, up from 3 hours 20 minutes in the prior quarter, and the last three nights each ran over 5 hours 30 minutes. Third, interview notes from the warehouse supervisor, who is a subject matter expert (SME), meaning a person with deep hands-on knowledge of the work. The supervisor said: the scanners come in batches and we have been told the first batch lands in week 12 at best. Complete these sub-tasks using only the inputs above. 1. Using the assumption log and the constraints, identify the assumption most likely to cascade into a threat to the six-hour sync window, and trace the chain of effects step by step from that assumption to the project objective it damages. 2. Write one risk trigger and one threshold for the sync-window risk. State the cause, the timing, the consequence, and the specific measurable value at which the team should act. 3. Classify the scanner delay and a possible faster sync as either threat or opportunity. For the scanner delay, give a probability rating, an impact rating, and an urgency rating, each with a one-line reason. 4. The telemetry trend is evidence that the sync risk is already happening, and the supervisor's comment is evidence about the scanner risk. Explain how you would record each in the risk register, and whether a symptom such as slow runs should get its own entry.
subParts: Trace the cascade from the export assumption to the sync window and the project objective
Write a trigger and threshold for the sync-window risk
Classify the scanner delay and faster sync, and rate the scanner delay
Record the telemetry and supervisor evidence in the register without duplicate entries
modelAnswer: The most likely cascade starts with the assumption that the export tool moves all 1.2 million records in one pass. If the tool must split records into batches, the export takes longer. A longer export pushes the full sync run later into the nightly window. The sync already averages 4 hours 10 minutes against a 6-hour constraint, so the extra export time eats the safety margin. If the sync runs past 5 a.m., warehouse staff open the building with stale stock counts, which damages the objective of accurate stock data at go-live. The learner should name the export assumption, then show each link: split batches, longer export, less margin, overrun, stale data, objective damaged.

A good trigger is the cause that signals the risk is starting: record volume growth combined with export batch splitting, checked on every nightly run during testing and after cutover. A good threshold is a measurable value set before the hard limit, so the team has time to react. For example, act when any two consecutive nights exceed 5 hours 30 minutes, or when the rolling seven-night average exceeds 5 hours. The consequence to state is that the stock figures will not be ready by the 5 a.m. opening. The threshold sits below the 6-hour constraint on purpose, because waiting until the limit is breached leaves no room to fix the problem.

The scanner delay is a threat, because it is an uncertain event that would hurt the project if it happens. A faster sync gained from a vendor fix would be an opportunity, because it is an uncertain event that would help. For the scanner delay, probability is high, since the vendor's best case is week 12 against an assumed week 10. Impact is medium to high, since cutover and testing would slip and the schedule and any dependent work would move. Urgency is high, since the schedule decision has to be made before week 10 arrives. Ratings are professional judgment and should be stated with reasons.

Each risk gets one register entry. The sync risk gets one entry, and the telemetry trend is recorded as evidence and an indicator attached to that entry, not as a second risk. The scanner risk gets its own entry, and the supervisor's comment is attached to it as evidence. Slow job runs are a symptom: the underlying risk is the cause, such as record volume and batch splitting. Creating a separate entry for the symptom would double-count one problem, distort the risk ranking, and make the response plan harder to follow.

scenarios.title: Warehouse Picking System Upgrade at Harbor Crest Supply
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Crest Supply is a fictional regional distributor with two warehouses. Its project manager, Dana, is replacing the order-picking software that tells staff which items to collect and in what order. The project budget is $1.2 million and the target go-live is 16 weeks away. Dana's team has a risk breakdown structure (RBS), which is a tree that groups risks by source, such as technology, people, vendors, and finance, so every risk has a home category. The team has logged three open risks. Risk A: the new system may not work with the older barcode scanner drivers used on the warehouse floor. If it happens, the team estimates a 60,000 dollar rework cost and a one-week delay, and the team's best estimate of the chance of it happening is 40 percent. Risk B: the lead data engineer may resign before go-live. This would cost about 90,000 dollars in contractor fees and a three-week slip, and the chance is low. Risk C: the cloud host may raise prices at renewal, adding about 15,000 dollars, and the chance is moderate. The team uses a 5 by 5 risk matrix, which is a grid that scores each risk by probability (how likely it is, scored 1 to 5) multiplied by impact (how bad it is for objectives such as cost, time, or quality, scored 1 to 5). Dana also has a choice to make. A compatibility tool costs 20,000 dollars and removes Risk A completely, while accepting the risk leaves it in place. Finally, the sponsor wants to know the likely finish date, and the schedule has three tasks with uncertain durations that the team has estimated as ranges. Answer the following. 1. Using the scores in the scenario, assign each of Risks A, B, and C a probability score and an impact score from 1 to 5 on the matrix, multiply them to get each risk's score, and rank the three risks from highest to lowest priority. Briefly justify the ranking in terms of impact and urgency. 2. For Risk A, calculate the expected monetary value (EMV) of accepting the risk and compare it with the cost of the compatibility tool. State which option Dana should choose on expected cost and say what the decision tree would show. 3. The sponsor asks for a single finish date. Explain why the team should run a Monte Carlo simulation, which is a method that repeatedly samples random durations for each uncertain task to build a spread of possible finish dates, rather than adding up the most likely durations. State what output the team should report to the sponsor.
subParts: Rank Risks A, B and C on the 5 by 5 matrix with justification
Calculate EMV for accepting Risk A and compare with the tool cost, state the decision
Explain why Monte Carlo is used and what finish-date output to report
modelAnswer: Definition first: a risk matrix scores each risk as probability times impact, so a higher product means a higher priority. Risk A: probability 4 (the team's 40 percent is a likely-to-happen chance, so 4 on the 5 point scale) and impact 3 (a one-week delay and 60,000 dollars is moderate), giving a score of 12. Risk B: probability 2 (low chance) and impact 4 (three weeks and 90,000 dollars is severe), giving 8. Risk C: probability 3 (moderate chance) and impact 2 (15,000 dollars is minor), giving 6. Ranking: A (12) first, then B (8), then C (6). Justification: A is both likely and close in time, so it is also the most urgent because it would hit during build and testing before go-live. B is less likely but has the largest single delay, so it stays high on the list and needs a backup plan. C matters least and can wait for the renewal date. A common mistake is ranking only by impact and ignoring probability. A matrix score is only a ranking tool, not a precise measure of money.

Definition first: expected monetary value, or EMV, is the probability of a risk multiplied by its money impact. It turns uncertainty into one expected cost. Why it works: it lets two options be compared on the same scale. Step by step for accepting Risk A: probability 0.40 (40 percent, written as a decimal, not 40); impact 60,000 dollars; EMV = 0.40 times 60,000 = 24,000 dollars. For mitigating with the tool: a fixed cost of 20,000 dollars, and the tool removes Risk A, so its residual EMV is zero, giving a total of 20,000 dollars. A decision tree is a diagram with branches for each choice and each chance outcome; for this decision it has one decision node (buy the tool or accept) and, on the accept branch, one chance node (risk occurs at 0.40, or does not at 0.60). Its result is 24,000 dollars for accepting versus 20,000 dollars for buying, so buying the tool is the lower expected cost by 4,000 dollars. The common mistake is writing 40 in place of 0.40, which multiplies the impact by 40 and gives an absurd answer; another is forgetting the tool cost in the mitigation branch. A sensible recommendation mentions that the EMV favours the tool, and that the tool also protects the schedule, which EMV alone does not capture.

Definition first: a Monte Carlo simulation is a method that runs thousands of random trials. In each trial it picks a duration for every uncertain task from the range the team gave, then adds the durations along the schedule path to get one possible finish date. Why it works: the schedule risk is not simply the sum of the most likely durations, because some tasks running long together makes the project finish much later than the typical case, and a single average hides that. Worked example: suppose three tasks each have a most likely duration of 4 weeks, but a range of 3 to 8 weeks. Adding the most likely values gives 12 weeks, yet across many trials the finish is spread out, with a tail reaching well past 12 weeks. The output is a distribution of finish dates. The team reports a confidence level, such as the P80 date, which is the date by which the project finishes in 80 percent of trials, and gives the spread, such as P50 and P80. A common mistake is reporting only the most likely or average finish, which makes the schedule look safer than it is. Consequence for the running system: if the sponsor commits to a go-live date based on the 12-week sum, a late finish could disrupt warehouse operations, so the team should present the P80 date and explain it, together with the tasks that drive the spread.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Foods: Responding to a Data Migration Risk
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Foods is a fictional mid-sized packaged-food company. Its project team is moving the order-scheduling system from an old on-site server to a new cloud platform in ten weeks. The team's risk register (a shared list of identified risks with their scores and status) includes this entry: the old system's nightly export script may fail to carry customer delivery windows (the agreed days and hours a customer can receive goods) into the new system, so some orders could ship on the wrong day. The likelihood is medium and the impact is high. Priya Nair is the project's risk lead, and each risk has a named owner who is accountable for its actions. The steering group (the senior managers who approve budget and scope) has asked for a plan. Please answer the following.

1. Choose one response strategy for this risk from avoid, accept, mitigate, enhance, or contingency. Briefly define the strategy you choose in your own words, justify why it fits this risk, and list at least two time-bound actions, each with a named owner and a due date.

2. Four weeks into the project, the team tracks this risk weekly on a burndown chart (a line chart that plots remaining risk exposure over time against a planned downward target line). The actual line has stayed flat for two weeks while the target line keeps falling. Explain what this pattern tells the steering group about the response, and describe what you would communicate and what you would change.

3. In week seven, a test reconciliation shows that 3 percent of delivery windows do not match between the old and new systems. The pre-agreed trigger for the contingency plan (a fallback plan activated only when a stated condition occurs, here any mismatch above 1 percent) has been met, so the team activates the contingency: warehouse leads manually check the next day's shipments each evening. Describe the steps needed to implement this contingency properly, then evaluate one secondary risk (a new risk created by the response) and the residual risk (the risk that remains after the response is applied).
subParts: Choose a response strategy, justify it, and assign time-bound actions with owners
Explain the flat burndown chart and what to communicate and change
Implement the contingency and evaluate a secondary risk and the residual risk
modelAnswer: Strong answer: Choose mitigate, because the team can reduce the likelihood or impact of the mismatch without removing the migration itself (avoid would mean cancelling the migration, and accept would ignore a high-impact risk). Mitigate means taking steps that lower the chance or size of the risk. Justify it by noting that the risk can be reduced by checking the export before cutover. Time-bound actions could include: the data engineer, Marcus Lee, writes a reconciliation script that compares every delivery window between old and new systems, due in week 3; Priya Nair schedules a test migration of one week of orders, due in week 5; the warehouse operations lead, Dana Ortiz, confirms the list of customer delivery windows that must be checked, due in week 4. Each action needs one named owner and a date, so progress can be checked. Common mistake: naming a strategy with no actions, or actions with no owner or deadline. Consequence: nobody is answerable when the due date passes, so the risk stays unmanaged.

Strong answer: A burndown chart shows whether the response is reducing exposure. A flat actual line while the target falls means the response is not working as planned, even though work may be happening. The steering group should hear that the mitigation has not yet lowered the risk score, that the reason is likely that the reconciliation script is late or not yet run against real data, and that the expected reduction is at risk. Communicate in plain terms: the risk is not shrinking on schedule, the cause, the date by which the team will know more, and the decision needed if the gap continues. Change the plan by bringing forward the test migration, reassigning the script work if needed, and adding a checkpoint at the next weekly review. Common mistake: reporting that work is ongoing as if it proves reduction. Consequence: the steering group keeps approving the plan while exposure stays high.

Strong answer: Implementing a contingency means carrying out a fallback only after its trigger is confirmed, not guessing. Steps: first, confirm the trigger by checking that the reconciliation result really exceeds 1 percent and record the evidence; second, notify the risk owner and the steering group that the contingency is active; third, assign warehouse leads to check each evening's shipments against the delivery windows list, with a written checklist and a named coordinator; fourth, set a review date to decide when the contingency can stop. A secondary risk is that manual checks add workload and introduce human error, so leads may tire or miss mismatches; mitigate that with rota cover and a second check on high-value orders. The residual risk is the mismatch risk that remains even with manual checks, for example if a mismatch is found after shipment; state that residual risk to the steering group and agree who accepts it. Common mistake: treating a contingency as a permanent strategy or forgetting to evaluate new risks it creates. Consequence: the workaround quietly becomes the process while staff burn out and errors go unrecorded.

scenarios.title: Warehouse System Move: Monitoring and Closing Risks Before Cutover
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Freight is a fictional regional logistics company moving its warehouse tracking from an old on-site system to a cloud-hosted system called the Move Project. A cloud-hosted system is one run by an outside vendor over the internet, so Brightwater does not manage the servers itself. Risk R-07, 'vendor data migration may corrupt pallet records', was scored high during analysis. The chosen response was a parallel run: for three weeks both systems record every shipment, and the team compares them each day before switching off the old system. Parallel run means running the old and new systems side by side so one can check the other. You are the project's risk lead, and it is now week 6 of a 10-week plan. Work package WP-4.2 ('parallel-run reconciliation', meaning the task of comparing the two systems' records) had a planned budget of 40 hours and a planned duration of 3 weeks. Actual effort is 52 hours, and the reconciliation is about 1 week behind. Daily mismatch counts fell from 120 to 8 over two weeks, but on the most recent day 14 shipments appeared where the cloud system shows a delivery timestamp in a different time zone and the old system does not. The vendor's release notes say a patch will fix time-zone handling, but no patch date is confirmed. At the last status meeting R-07 was closed with the note 'mitigated'. The register also holds R-11, 'staff unfamiliar with new system', with an expiry date of last Friday because training has finished. The steering group meets Thursday and will receive a one-page summary. Complete these tasks: 1. Perform a variance analysis on WP-4.2, explain what the hours and schedule variances tell you about monitoring effort, and state which data you would reconcile before trusting the mismatch count. 2. Identify the residual or secondary risk created by the time-zone mismatch after the parallel-run response, state how you would track it, and describe what you would tell the steering group about its impact. 3. Specify the updates you would make to the risk register, the change log and the lessons learned record, including how you would handle R-07 and the expired R-11. 4. Set the overall project risk level for the steering summary and explain what that summary should contain for a steering group, as opposed to the detailed risk report the project team uses.
subParts: Variance analysis of WP-4.2 and data reconciliation before trusting the mismatch count
Residual or secondary risk from the time-zone mismatch: tracking and steering group impact
Risk register, change log and lessons learned updates, including R-07 and expired R-11
Overall project risk level and tailored steering group reporting
modelAnswer: A variance is the difference between what was planned and what actually happened, calculated as actual minus planned. Here the hours variance is 52 minus 40, which equals 12 hours over plan, or 30 percent. The schedule variance is about 1 week behind plan. Both numbers matter for monitoring because extra hours spent on a risk-related work package usually mean the response is harder to run than expected, and a schedule slip means the cutover date is at risk. Before trusting the mismatch count of 8, reconcile three things: that the count covers every shipment in the parallel-run window rather than a sample; that both systems' timestamps are converted to the same time zone before comparison, since the 14 new mismatches show this was not done consistently; and that the work package scope matches the risk response scope, so no shipment types are left out. A mistake would be to report the falling count as proof the risk is down. If the comparison itself is flawed, the cutover could go ahead with corrupted delivery records that nobody can trace back.

A residual risk is the risk left over after a response has been carried out, and a secondary risk is a new risk created by the response itself. The time-zone mismatch is best treated as a residual risk of R-07, because the parallel run is still exposing data that the migration does not yet handle correctly, and as a secondary risk tied to the vendor, because the fix depends on a patch with no confirmed date. Track it by opening a separate register entry with an owner, a trigger (for example, any day with time-zone mismatches above zero after the patch is due), and a daily count of mismatches of this type, plus a weekly check of the vendor's patch status. For the steering group, state the impact in plain terms: 14 shipments currently show wrong delivery times, the cause is known, the fix depends on an unconfirmed vendor date, and the cutover can only proceed safely once the mismatch count for this type is zero or a documented workaround is approved. Avoid saying the risk is handled simply because most mismatches are gone; the group needs to know which problem is still open and what decision it affects.

Update the risk register by re-opening R-07 with status 'residual risk open' rather than 'mitigated', because the parallel run has shown the response is not complete, and by adding the new time-zone risk as a linked entry with its owner, trigger and review date. Mark R-11 as closed rather than deleting it: record the closure reason (training finished, with the training completion evidence attached) and the date, so the history remains available for audits. The change log should record the vendor patch as a dependency and any change to the cutover date or the parallel-run window, with the reason and approver for each. The lessons learned record should note that time-zone handling was not tested before the parallel run began, so the team should add a test of timestamp conversion to future migration plans, and should note that R-07 was closed early based on a falling count. Closing a risk because its count dropped, without checking whether the cause is resolved, is a common mistake. The consequence here is that the cutover could go live with wrong delivery times, causing customer disputes and manual correction work that the register would not show.

Overall project risk level should be set using the project's agreed rating scale. Here the level should move from moderate to high until the time-zone issue is resolved or a workaround is approved, because one open issue directly affects data correctness at cutover and depends on an outside party. The steering summary should be short and written in business terms: the current overall rating and its direction (rising, steady or falling), the two or three risks that most affect the decision, the schedule and hours impact already seen, the specific decisions needed from the group (for example, whether to hold the cutover date, approve a manual check workaround, or accept the residual risk formally), and the date of the next update. The detailed risk report kept by the project team, by contrast, lists every register entry with scores, response actions, owners and triggers. A steering group does not need that level of detail, and giving it the full register would hide the decision it has to make. A common mistake is sending the full register to the steering group, or sending only a green overall status that omits the open time-zone issue.
